title: Theories are never true, they are only more or less useful
subtitle: Everything you believe is wrong
author: Manuel Delaflor
introduction: We think our theories about reality – whether in physics, philosophy, or psychology – should aspire to be faithful descriptions of how reality actually is. But philosopher of science Manuel Delaflor makes the case that this aspiration is incredibly dangerous. Instead of thinking our theories map onto an underlying reality, Delaflor asks us to stop worshipping our models, even though we cannot stop modelling any more than we can stop breathing. Evaluating our theories by what they can do, and not by what they claim to be, will make us far more productive and happier.
body:
There is a moment, just before you fully wake, when you don't know who you are. For a breath or two, there is experience without a name attached to it. No nationality. No profession. No opinions about immigration or breakfast cereals. Just… this... sensation without stubborn content. This can also happen when having a peak experience, an awe where everything feels… different, that cannot be put into words. And then the labels arrive, one after another, like apps loading on a phone, and within seconds you are yourself again: your name, your worries, your convictions, your plans for Tuesday. The moment passes so quickly that most people never notice it happened. But something was there before the naming began. Something that needed no beliefs to sustain it. I want to talk about that something. But in order to do that properly, first, I need to talk about everything we pile on top of it.

Beliefs, certainties, ideologies, even the day-by-day heuristics that allow you to function as a person. And what I find interesting is that all of that, all of it, everything you believe you know—is wrong. Not approximately wrong. Not wrong in the details while right in spirit. Wrong in a way that cannot be fixed by swapping one belief for a better one, wrong in the deepest possible sense that language cannot even touch, because the error is not in the content of your beliefs but in the act of believing itself, the assumption about any symbolic structure can faithfully represent what it claims to describe.

Your beliefs about God are wrong. Your beliefs about science are wrong. Your beliefs about yourself, your country, your childhood, your future—wrong, wrong, wrong. Wrong. And before the objections start arriving, let me be clear: mine are too. And no, this is not a new set of beliefs that “are true” that I am trying to “teach” you or shove down your throat. And no, this is also not cynicism. If anything, it is better to say that this is a diagnosis. And the prescription, I promise, is not despair.

A belief is a stabilization mechanism. It takes the roaring, kaleidoscopic flood of experience and holds one frame still long enough for you to act on it.

Now, before I can continue, I believe it is pertinent to make a small pause, because I can almost hear you already thinking, “but I know how to ride a bike, is that wrong?” No. Because “I can ride a bike” is not a belief in the sense that matters here. It is an operative competence, a description of something you can do. It makes no claim about what bikes are, what balance is, what you are. Same with “2+2=4,” which is a rule inside a formal system that works impeccably within its own constraints. My proposed epistemic stance—Model Dependent Ontology, or MDO—does not touch these. What MDO dismantles are the beliefs that claim to tell you what things are. “I am an introvert.” “Matter is the fundamental substrate.” “The universe was created with purpose.” These are ontological claims, claims about the nature of what exists, and they are everywhere, hiding inside beliefs that look as innocent as knowing how to ride a bike. The distinction is everything: an operative heuristic says, “this works.” An ontological belief says, “this is how things are.” The first one is a tool. The second one is a cage.

Consider what a belief actually is. Not what it claims to be (a faithful portrait of how things stand, or how things are, or what they are) … let’s focus on what it does. A belief is a stabilization mechanism. It takes the roaring, kaleidoscopic flood of experience and holds one frame still long enough for you to act on it. It is a photograph of a river, useful precisely because it stops the flow, and wrong precisely because the river never stops. Every belief you hold performs this trick. “I am an introvert.” Useful shorthand. Freezes a thousand contradictory moments into a manageable label. But attend closely to your actual experience across a single week and the label starts to crack. You were gregarious at dinner. You were withdrawn at the meeting. You were electric with old friends and mute with strangers. The label does not describe you. It replaces you with something more convenient, and then you live as though the convenience were the fact.

This is a monstrosity if you ask me. You become the photograph and forget you were ever a river. Consider the simplistic belief that infinite complexity across countless dimensions can fit onto a small label. If you expand this idea, the implications are staggering. Nations are beliefs. Borders are beliefs. Money is a belief so deeply entrenched that people starve in its name while surrounded by food, shelter, and willing hands, just because the token system says so. Imagine watching this from the outside, a species that can feed itself choosing not to, because a number in a ledger doesn’t allow them. The belief has become the warden. The inmates don't notice, because the prison is made of blind consensus. Don’t think, believe.

Certainty, in this light, is a seizure. It is what happens when a model grips the modeller so tightly that the modeller forgets there was ever a choice.

Keep zooming out and multiply this by every belief system that has ever claimed authority over human life. Religious systems tell you “what the cosmos means,” who “made it,” and what happens when you die. Political systems tell you how power “should be distributed,” what laws you must follow, and who “deserves” what. Scientific frameworks tell you what counts as “evidence” and which methods are “legitimate.” Philosophical traditions tell you what questions are “worth” asking and which answers are “admissible.” Each of these is a stabilization of the unnameable infinite into the tamed shame of what is named and reduced to a caricature. Humans capture the river in an image of ridiculous quality and suddenly assert with a squeal that the photograph is the river. “This is how things are,” with a prideful smirk.

But… These systems do not describe anything, because to “describe” they first need to claim to “know” what is “that” that is “being described.” What these systems do is conscript. A tiny label becomes the master of your destiny. And the moment a belief achieves enough social mass… people begin to defend it not because they have freshly examined its merits but because their very sense of identity is fused to it, because abandoning it would feel like dying, like self-betrayal. This is why political arguments generate more heat than light. This is why theological debates have launched wars. This is why people will look at overwhelming evidence against their position and experience it as an attack on their person. The belief has hijacked the believer. The actual individual died long before.

Certainty, in this light, is a seizure. It is what happens when a model grips the modeller so tightly that the modeller forgets there was ever a choice. And the more certain you are, the less you can see, because certainty becomes the process by which the toolkit becomes invisible to the hand that wields it. One of the reasons I developed Model Dependent Ontology was to do something that all realist ideologies failed to do: it stops engaging the war that cannot be won. The war is this: decide which picture of the world is the “right one.” Decide which ontology is “really real.” Materialism or idealism? Physicalism or dualism? Substance or process? For millennia, brilliant minds have fought this war. And where has it landed? Nowhere. Not one inch closer to resolution. Every generation produces new arguments for the same positions, and every generation believes it has finally clinched “it,” and every subsequent generation proves it hadn't. The history of ontological philosophy is not the slow, steady and heroic march towards “truth,” not even when humans developed its branch called science. Ontology is a magnificent machinery feeding endless superstitions without end. Even the pragmatist, who claims to only care about what works, is secretly praying that “what works” is a whisper from the Real. MDO makes no such prayer. It embraces the silence. It does not stop to ask which ontology is “the right one.” It does not adjudicate between competing pictures of what the universe is “made of.” It asks a different question entirely, the question that actually gets us somewhere: what can we achieve with this model?

Where does it work? Where does it break? What does it predict? What does it miss? Which constraints does it respect and which does it ignore? It is operational discipline. It is the reason science advances while every other castle made of human beliefs goes round in circles of doom. Science, if we use it correctly, is not there to tell us which models are ontologically correct. MDO insists that the one and only thing that matters is that they must be operationally accountable. A model must make predictions. Those predictions must be testable. When they fail, the model is revised or replaced. And so the question is never “is this model the final portrait of how things are?” The question is always “does this model do the job we need it to do within the constraints we can identify?”

The personality you defend, the autobiography you tell at dinner parties, the self-image that keeps you up at night—these are models. Useful ones, often. But models nonetheless.

This is epistemically efficient. It is the only approach in the history of human thought that has consistently generated cumulative, revisable understanding. And it achieves this precisely by refusing to make ontological commitments. The physicist does not need to know whether electrons are “really real” to use quantum electrodynamics to predict measurements to twelve decimal places. The engineer does not need a metaphysics of matter to build a bridge that carries trucks. The operational question, what can the model do?,  is the question that builds civilizations. The ontological question, what is the model really describing?, is the question that leads to wars.

Let me be brutally specific. If you are a materialist who insists that matter is the fundamental substrate, I have a question: what is matter? You will say particles. What are particles? You will say quantum fields. What are quantum fields? You will say mathematical structures that describe measurable interactions. And there it is. You have just described what your model does, what it measures, what it predicts… not what the world is. If you are an idealist who insists that mind or consciousness is fundamental, the same question applies. What is consciousness? You will offer a definition. What grounds the definition? Another one, then another framework, until you get to an answer denoting a use. Every attempt to state what the world fundamentally “is” turns out, upon a deep and honest examination, to be a description of what some model fundamentally does. And once you accept the operating condition, you stop wasting energy on the impossible and start investing it in what matters: building better models, understanding their limitations, knowing when to switch between them, and… crucially… never mistaking any of them for the last word.

But notice what this also does to you. Personally. Intimately. If every belief is a stabilization, and every stabilization is a photograph of a river, then you, the you that you take yourself to be, is also a tiny, badly taken photograph. The story of who you are, compiled over decades from memory, habit, and repetition, is a construction. And like all constructions, it has edges, distortions, and blind spots. The personality you defend, the autobiography you tell at dinner parties, the self-image that keeps you up at night—these are models. Useful ones, often. But models nonetheless. You are not who you think you are. Not because some truer self is hiding underneath, waiting to be found. If you have ever stood at the edge of an ocean at night and felt, for just a moment, that the categories dissolved… that the separation between you and the dark water and the stars was a kind of agreed-upon fiction… you have already tasted it. If you have ever watched a child encounter something genuinely novel, and seen in their face an astonishment that has no name, no box, no framework, just sheer, unprocessed meeting with the new… you have seen it at work. That awe, a silent awareness, speaks more of you than any of your highly treasured beliefs.

SUGGESTED READING Truth is the most dangerous fantasy our species ever invented By Manuel Delaflor

The world, stripped of all the labels we paste onto it, is unspeakably full, infinitely complex, beyond terrifying, and transcendentally beautiful. The error of nihilism is to assume that without our categories, nothing remains. The error of realism is to assume that our categories capture what remains. Both errors come from the same place: treating the map as though it were, or should be, the territory. MDO suggests something more radical and, I believe, more humble: maps are navigational tools. They are magnificent, indispensable for getting us from here to there, for predicting, for coordinating, for building. But the thing they navigate, the raw, unprocessed what-is-happening… is not itself a map. It is not organized into the neat categories we project onto it. It is, in a word that realists will hate, a miracle. Not a supernatural one. A natural one. Try to think about it without your spine shivering… The sheer improbability of anything happening at all.

This is what the moment before waking touches. Before the labels load. Before the apps boot up. Before you become your name and your worries and your beliefs about the economy. There is something there… unnameable… prior to everything we say about it. And it is, if you let it be, an invitation. To see, not to believe, not to assess, not to reason about it… to SEE how everything you believe is wrong. Useful as they may be, your beliefs are stabilizations that inevitably distort everything they touch. This is not cause for despair. It is cause for something far more profound: absolute contact.

MDO does not tell you to stop modelling. You cannot stop modelling any more than you can stop breathing. It only asks you to stop worshipping your models. To evaluate them by what they can do, not by what they claim to be. To hold them with the lightness of tools, not the ferocity of identities. And to remember, always, that beneath every model, every label, every belief, there is something that was never captured, never named, never right, and never wrong. Because it was never the kind of thing that needed a name.
